region_scene_page.compact: A downtown New York scene/ecosystem where punk urgency, art-school experiment, poetry, pop instincts, minimal electronics, and club culture collided around CBGB and nearby venues rather than resolving into one sound.
region_scene_page.standard: CBGB opened in 1973 on the Bowery under Hilly Kristal and became a practical home for original underground rock. What later looks like “the CBGB sound” was actually a cluster of incompatible but mutually intensifying bands: Patti Smith fused rock and poetry; Television stretched guitar interplay into nervous art-rock; Talking Heads turned anxiety, rhythm, and conceptual framing into new wave; Blondie smuggled girl-group/pop/disco instincts through downtown cool; Richard Hell gave punk a persona of damaged refusal; Suicide reduced rock to voice, synth pulse, and menace; and No Wave pushed the scene toward abrasive boundary testing. Scene before sound: bands shared rooms, audience, press, and permission structure more than a single musical grammar. Original-song rule: the venue became a testing ground for bands that did not fit cover-band or arena-rock economics. Art-punk plurality: poetry-rock, nervous funk, pop-art new wave, guitar abstraction, minimal synth menace, and No Wave abrasion all sit in the same historical neighborhood. Anti-classic-rock scale: short sets, small rooms, stripped gear, weird personas, and direct performance replaced virtuoso sprawl. Bridge behavior: the archetype points backward to first-wave punk/proto-punk and forward to post-punk, new wave, college rock, noise-rock, synth-punk, and indie art-rock. Fit caution: an Atlas user may love Blondie or Talking Heads while rejecting Suicide/No Wave, or love Television while rejecting broader punk.
